newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens sees Asian, European growth rising.
newsitem.headline: Siemens sees Asian, European growth rising.

text.p: German industrial group Siemens AG plans to expand sales in Asia by 20 percent a year and expects volumes of over 25 billion marks ($13.9 billion) by 2001, even though Asian profits in 1996/97 will be static.

Guenter Wilhelm, head of Siemens' Asia-Pacific activities, told a news conference the group expected 1996/97 after-tax profit in its Asian businesses to be about 300 million marks, unchanged from a year ago.
Results in the region in the year to the end of September 1997 would be dampened by a loss in its Indian unit.
"I think we have a loss (in India). The financial year is not over, I don't know how much it will be yet," Wilhelm said.
Wilhelm said he expected orders in Asia this year to increase to 10 billion marks, up from nine billion last year.
Emerging markets in the region were driving growth in sales of advanced communications and electronics technologies and large infrastructure projects.
"Today Asia Pacific is in the midst of an unprecendented boom, showing the world's most dynamic growth," Wilhelm said.

However, he said "it is hard to make money there", because of intense price competition. The group had three billion marks invested in the region, and this would rise to six billion by 2001, Wilhelm said.

Wilhelm's colleague on the management board, Juergen Radomski, said Siemens expected growth of 10 to 15 percent in Europe, not including Germany, in the next few years, with much of that coming from eastern Europe.
Radomski said he expected overall sales to grow to 130 billion marks by the year 2000, of which 55 percent was expected to come from Europe, compared to 66 percent last year.
Within European turnover, Germany would only contribute 50 percent, down from 58 percent last year.
The Asia Pacific region's contribution to turnover would rise to 20 percent from 17.
Radomski said that the group expected sales in western Europe, not including Germany, to rise to 26 billion marks in 1996/97 from the year-ago figure of 24.2 billion marks.
Siemens expected a further 10 billion marks from joint ventures, such as Italtel in Italy and GPT in Britain.

There were currently no discussions about Siemens taking over the GEC share of the GPT joint venture, nor were there discussions about changes at the Siemens GEC Communications joint venture in Britain, Radomski said.
There were no plans to start a joint venture with the French group Jeumont Schneider, although the groups were talking generally to each other, he said.
In the medium term, annual growth would be between 10 and 15 percent, Radomski said, faster than the overall market.
In eastern Europe, Siemens expected around 15 percent growth a year and Radomski said sales this year would rise to around four billion marks from 2.5 billion marks.

The group would invest around three billion marks to expand its European business, one billion more than last year. Deliveries from Siemens factories in Europe had grown to 13 billion marks from nine billion marks.

Radomski said the group would not be cutting the workforce to achieve its goals, and that Siemens expected a "sideways movement" in the personnel area. The group planned to incorporate more firms in Europe.
Siemens is due to release its nine-month results here on Monday.

($ = 1.797 German Marks)
